item.title: flipper gray
item.content:encoded:
Flipper gray is a dolphin-forward colloquial term for the dull paint which landlords and house flippers gleefully douse apartment walls in, the perfect shade to minimize sratchy upkeep and maximize the toiling renter lowest common denominator. Often, they leave just the windowsills and door frames intact -- taunting lines of eggshells and alabaster, salt and chiffon, cream and snow.

I recently moved from a flippery Boston Triple Decker into a converted warehouse loft building in Brooklyn called The Tea Factory. The source of this name is unclear -- a NYT article from 2008 claims the building was once the property of "Spice and Tea Exclusively Ltd", an entity with no search results besides the aforementioned article. It's a beautiful apartment with miraculously white walls, very tall ceilings, and a hallway stretching perpendicular to the street for so long and so wide it might as well be called a hall. The bedrooms run along the hall railroad style and the unit is in the center of the building, so we possess but two windows to the outside world -- one which marks the end of our glorious hall, and another six feet to its right in the "front" bedroom. Every bedroom has windows, though. In a fit of optimism, whoever assembled our chateau gave every room a window into each room it's adjacent to along with a window to the hall (spare the bathroom). It's a bizarre arrangement, one which doesn't serve much of a purpose nor do anyone any good.

I sleep in the bedroom farthest from the sun. If I don't have any lights on and the door is closed, it's almost pitch black. Some morning light trickles in thanks to my bizarre neighborly windows, but not enough to simulate a gentle sunrise. What it does simulate, however, is the sensation of laying down for a catnap at 4:15pm and waking up 20 quick minutes later but where's the sun? and you're sweaty and sooo bewildered and here's the cheerful chatter of your roommates washing their dinner dishware wafting in from the kitchen -- they do all of their dishes right after they finish eating (and if something's burnt, it's left to soak in warm soapy water) -- do you? -- the day's over, you blew it, shut your eyes and try again tomorrow. To mitigate the waking nightmare, I went to a hardware store and bought some timer outlets. Now, my bedside lamps switch on automatically at 7:30am, setting the stage for 7:45 sharp when WBGO 88.3FM blasts brashly from my radio alarm clock in an arc through the hoop balancing on the nose of the little wire seal sculpture perched at the foot of my bed and into my perforated eardrums no matter how gingerly I wind the volume knob towards 179° every previous evening. I set a lamp timer for the kitchen as well, as meekly fumbling through a shadowy kitchen and flipping various levers and switches to make the shadows go away every morning made me feel like a glum prisoner on an outer space mining colony.

At my previous apartment in Boston, I spent far too much time in my bedroom, working a very unpleasant full-time remote software engineer job. Every morning, I would wake up at 8am, make a feeble attempt to get up to work out or shower, and be coaxed back into sleep by my warm drowsy girlfriend. 55 minutes later, it's go time -- cram morning updates from India before Team Stupid logs off, join morning standup to get yelled at by the CEO's dad (???), then endeavor to get 3 or 4 hours of productive work done before being assigned to "own" any amount of URGENT tasks, piled on from 9am to midnight. The only reason it was bearable was because my room was huge and airy and got gorgeous light at all times of the day. My plants flourished under the glow of my stained glass hangers and sometimes the sunrise would beam into my bright red wooden office chair so fiercely that a bloody phantasm would come alive and dance across the walls, careening from vine to vine. I never took a picture.

item.title: the old vs. the newgrass pt.1
item.content:encoded:
There's a joke oft repeated on web forums for the Berklee College Of Music; when a new or prospective student inquires to the digital either about who the disheveled figures seen murmuring around the wooden benches bolted to the main campus buildings are, the ether types back:

"Alumni."

When I learned the Guitar Center situated directly across Mass Ave from those benches had closed, I was astonished. I could hardly picture a more convenient location for any business, beat out narrowly by the Microcenter near MIT or any 7-11 next to any high school anywhere. Pondering the margins brought it into focus -- Guitar Center and other big box music stores make most of their money selling brand new yet scratched up Telecasters to idiots such as myself, hideously overpriced A/V equipment to dads with dreams, and $300 guitar lessons to my friend Meg. Berklee students have all that shit, and they're already paying $80,000 a year for music lessons.

So, to hell with the Mass Ave Guitar Center, it was selling waves to the ocean. I suspect replacement guitar string packs made up 90% of transactions, and today my shock has shifted to marveling that none of the dozens of cafes, restaurants, or bodegas bordering its now-empty storefront have put up a tiny window kiosk stuffed with Ernie Ball Regular Slinky Nickle Wounds. But, to hell with those businesses, too (except for Pho Basil). The only spot I give any real weight to the cash flow of isn't across from Berklee, but up and around the corner, a few doors down on Boylston if you're facing the Fens.

(contd.)

item.title: a q(uick) q (line) q(uestion)
item.content:encoded:
This evening, while waiting for the M train to take me back to Brooklyn from dinner with my dad in Manhattan's so-called "Koreatown", I observed two identically formatted notifications of a temporary Q train restriction, written in English and Spanish respectively, posted upon a load-bearing pillar on the platform.

The English poster opened with the caption:

"No Q train between Brighton Beach and Stillwell Av. . ."

while the Spanish poster opened with:

"No habia servicio de la linea Q entre Brighton Beach y Stillwell Av. . ."

Why so many extra words for the Spanish version? El theorized it's because "Q" is a very common shorthand for "qué", which basically means "what" in Spanish. It's funny to imagine a rushed Hispanic commuter glance over at a sign to read:

"No WHAT between Brighton Beach and Stillwell Av. . ."
